Q P C R copies a selected D N A region while measuring fluorescence during cycling. Team 5 starts with a prepared 96-well plate. Your task is to inspect it, load it, programme the instrument, run the lesson and explain the result. Use WHY at any step to learn the reason behind the action.

WHY CHECK THE I D?
A plate has 96 wells: rows A through H and columns one through twelve. The label must match the handoff record so results are assigned to the correct experiment. Our record is T four, Q P C R, two zero two six, zero five. If it does not match, stop and resolve the discrepancy; do not guess.

WHY FIND A one?
A one means row A, column 1. It fixes the direction of the plate map. Rotating the plate 180 degrees puts samples under the wrong well names. Find the red corner now, and match it to the red corner on the holder during loading.

WHY AN OPTICAL SEAL?
A flat, intact seal keeps reactions enclosed and reduces evaporation during heating. It must transmit the light used for fluorescence measurements. Check edges and avoid touching the optical surface. If the seal is damaged or lifting, resolve it before loading.

WHY CHECK BUBBLES?
Bubbles can disturb optical readings. Team 5 receives an already prepared and sealed plate. If bubbles are present, follow the approved brief centrifugation procedure with a balanced plate centrifuge before loading. This lesson's plate is already ready; do not open it or remix its reactions.

WHY RETURN THE PLATE?
Put the sealed plate flat in its clean handoff position while preparing the machine. Carry it by its edges. A floor drop can damage or compromise it: the simulator leaves it on the floor and blocks loading until Reset provides a fresh training plate.

WHY POWER ON?
The electronics, optics and temperature controls must be ready before loading. A real instrument may perform startup checks; follow its manual. This simulator uses a short startup sound and welcome screen. The power button does not start amplification.

WHY OPEN THE COMPARTMENT?
The plate holder exposes the thermal block, which heats and cools the reactions. Wait for the drawer to stop moving. Never force it. Keep the sealed plate level and identify the holder's red A one corner before inserting it.

WHY ALIGN AND SEAT?
Match both A one corners and lower the plate flat into the holder. Correct seating provides contact with the temperature-controlled block and preserves the well map. Release Grip only when the guide turns green. Amber means misaligned; red explains a rejected attempt.

WHY CLOSE THE COMPARTMENT?
The plate must stay securely seated before the heated lid and thermal programme operate. The lid helps limit condensation; the enclosure supports consistent temperature and optical measurement. The simulator locks this action until seating succeeds.

WHY PROGRAM THE RUN?
The programme controls temperature, duration and fluorescence collection. Enter the temperatures AND hold times. This is a specified teaching assay using sigh-ber Green, not a universal recipe. A real assay requires validated primer, reagent and instrument instructions. Select a field for its explanation.

The programme controls temperature, duration and fluorescence collection. Enter the temperatures AND hold times. This is a specified teaching assay using sigh-ber Green, not a universal recipe. A real assay requires validated primer, reagent and instrument instructions. Select a field for its explanation.

WHY VALIDATE BEFORE START?
Confirm identity, seal, orientation, seating, closed drawer and every programme entry. The run repeatedly heats and cools reactions and measures fluorescence. A wrong setting can cause failed or misleading results. Real experiments also require appropriate controls and replicates.

WHAT IS HAPPENING?
At 95 degrees Celsius the D N A strands separate. At 60 degrees Celsius primers bind; fluorescence is collected. At 72 degrees Celsius the polymerase extends D N A. sigh-ber Green reports double-stranded D N A, including unwanted products. Watch the blue positive control, green teaching sample and orange N T C. Time is accelerated and all curves are synthetic teaching data.

HOW DO WE READ THE RESULT?
C Q (also called C T) is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a chosen threshold above background. The positive control should amplify; the N T C contains no template and should not show target amplification. Inspect melt peaks for unexpected products. One peak supports consistency but does not prove target identity. These checks do not replace full assay acceptance criteria.

WHAT HAVE YOU LEARNED?
You checked the handoff, aligned and loaded a sealed plate, programmed temperatures and hold times, monitored fluorescence and interpreted controls, C Q and a melt peak. Keep post P C R plates sealed to reduce carryover contamination. Use the laboratory's validated procedure for disposal and real experiments.

Reaction volume

Reaction volume is the amount in each well, not the whole plate. Enter 20 microlitres to match this prepared plate and the instrument's thermal settings.

Lid temperature

The heated lid is set to 105 degrees Celsius in this lesson. It helps limit condensation above the reactions. The lid temperature differs from the block temperature.

Initial denaturation

The initial hold is 95 degrees Celsius for 120 seconds. It separates D N A strands; activation requirements depend on the chosen polymerase. Use the validated reagent protocol.

Amplification cycles

Repeat the thermal sequence 35 times. Fluorescence is sampled each cycle. More cycles do not automatically mean a better or more reliable result.

Denaturation

Denaturation is 95 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds in each cycle. Heating separates the D N A strands so primers can bind in the next stage.

Annealing

Annealing is 60 degrees Celsius for 30 seconds in this teaching assay. Primers bind to complementary D N A. The appropriate temperature depends on primer design and assay validation.

Extension

Extension is 72 degrees Celsius for 30 seconds here. The D N A polymerase extends the primers to make new strands. Required time depends on the enzyme and product length.

Fluorescence acquisition

Acquire fluorescence at 60 degrees Celsius during annealing in each cycle. Comparing readings at the same stage provides a consistent amplification trace.

Melt curve start

After amplification, increase temperature from 65 to 95 degrees Celsius in zero point five degree steps. D N A melting changes sigh-ber fluorescence. A derivative peak shows a melting transition; extra peaks can indicate unwanted products. Dwell time follows the real instrument's method.
